Question:
Two right circular cones with vertices facing down as shown in the figure below contain the same amount of liquid. The radii of the tops of the liquid surfaces are \(3\) cm and \(6\) cm. Into each cone is dropped a spherical marble of radius \(1\) cm, which sinks to the bottom and is completely submerged without spilling any liquid. What is the ratio of the rise of the liquid level in the narrow cone to the rise of the liquid level in the wide cone?

[Figure 1](figures/2021_AMC_10A_Q12_question_fig1.svg)
Solution:
Compare the cones at equal occupied volumes, both before and after the marble is added. Initially the liquid volumes agree. Since cone volume is \(\pi r^2h/3\), the liquid heights \(h_1,h_2\) satisfy
\[
3^2h_1=6^2h_2,
\qquad h_1=4h_2.
\]
Each marble is completely submerged, so each raises the occupied volume from the same liquid volume \(V\) to the same larger volume \(V+4\pi/3\).

Within a fixed cone, the portions below two horizontal levels are similar cones. Multiplying their height by a factor \(t\) multiplies every length by \(t\), so their volume multiplies by \(t^3\). Because the volume multiplier is the same in both cones, the height multiplier \(t\) is the same too.

The rises are consequently \((t-1)h_1\) and \((t-1)h_2\). Their ratio is \(h_1:h_2=\boxed{4:1}\), choice E. Equal added volumes do not give equal rises; the cones' similar cross sections control the ratio.
